ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: the gods in the world
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: What the gods do beyond the colony's walls and to it: letters that swear by them, holy wars and relics, pilgrims and seers, champions, fevers broken and anger shown, gifts with a price, the void's bargains, and the quarrels of the gods themselves.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Every act of a god is remembered on its page (region window, Peoples, Gods). The words "some say" mean the gods are Felt; "the colony believes" that they are only Believed.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: The gods are behind what happens in the world, and the colony reads them into it. Neighbours swear by them in their letters and fight their wars for them; pilgrims come to pray at places on the colony's land; a god of war sends its champion; a god that favours the colony offers one of its people a gift, and names its price; one it is angry with shows it. Every act says whose hand it was, in the voice of how real the gods are, and plays out on the map.

points.li: Neighbours' letters tell of their god by what is true at their town: a sign of its favour when the town thrives, its anger when it struggles or mourns, an old myth of it and the god it is tied to, a war they fight as their god's quarrel. Sermons, stories and chronicles each have their own way of telling it.
Now and then a friend invites the colony to their god's feast. A gift of silver carried out to the gate pleases them and their god; the colony's regrets cost little.

A colony letter written by someone whose own god is the reader's god's rival, or by a scoffer, may slight their god. The words are in the letter, and their answer says they took offence: their goodwill and their god's favour fall, and the god may remember the writer.

Peoples who share a god get on better: once a season a people whose god is one of the colony's own, or one it stands pleased with, thinks a little better of it. A people whose god is the rival of a patron that favours the colony thinks a little worse, never below its own floor.
A holy war: a friend at war with a people whose god is their god's rival asks the colony to stand with them, send help, or stay out.
A temple's envoy comes to the gate for a relic the colony holds that is holy to their god: given, the envoy walks to it and carries it home; prayed over, they kneel by it an hour; refused, they go.

A people may call a place on the colony's land holy: an old tree (the anima or Gauranlen tree first), a river's bank, a crash site or an ancient machine, the colony's graves, an old ruin. Its pilgrims camp near it a few days, pray there at dawn and dusk, and leave nothing behind. The colony may join their dusk prayers or send them a meal. If the place is destroyed while they are there, they leave in grief, and their god is displeased.

A hermit seer may camp at the edge of the land for a month. Every few days the seer says what they see, and it is always true: a quarrel in the sky, a god's grudge against one of the colony, the Hunger coming for its due. Anyone who goes to sit by the seer's fire comes back with the colony's standing with every god it knows.

A raid by a people with a war god may be led by its champion, a fighter who will not easily go down. Beating the champion (dead, down or taken) is a sign: the war god's rivals and the colony's own war gods are pleased; a proud war god is impressed.

li.heading: Kindness and anger, at the game's own rate

points.li: In the small hours a fever may break or a plague ease for one who is ill, by the colony's standing with its god of healing: it only eases, never cures outright, and comes once an illness.

A god that holds a grudge against one colonist (who killed its sacred beast, or mocked it in a letter) may strike: a storm god's lightning on the roof over them in the next thunderstorm, landing clear of anyone; a wild, hunting or war god's wolves sent after them the next time they are out.

A god the colony has displeased at a home acts now and then by its nature: the game's own blight on the fields for the harvest and the waters, the sun put out an afternoon for the night, the dead and the void, a strike on an empty field in a storm. A patient or cold god never strikes.
Every hurt counts in Rimfolk's one budget of hurts from everyday life, so the gods never make the game crueller than it is.

A god that favours the colony may offer one of its people a lasting gift, spaced with the peoples' gifts: a blessing of its domain on their body (a blessed hand, storm-sense, a healer's touch, road-luck), a beast of its own, tame and bonded, or its relic (the colony faith's own lost relic with Ideology).

With A RimWorld of Magic, a class fitting the god: Priest or Paladin for healing, Druid for the wild, Ranger for the hunt, Geomancer for the Deep Mother, Necromancer or Death Knight for the dead and the Hunger, Storm Born for storms, Enchanter for the forge, Technomancer for machines, Bard for the night, Gladiator or Monk for war; a single spell or a gifted trait for one who already casts. With Royalty and Vanilla Psycasts Expanded, a psylink and a path.

Every gift has a price, named before the colony answers: silver carried out and left for the god, the god's mark, years of life, a cut taken there and then, or the anger of its rivals. Accepted, the colonist walks out under the open sky to receive it.
A trickster's gift turns to a curse after a while, and back. A rival the colony knows may send its avatar to the gate to undo a gift: let it, or send it off and earn its grudge.

Two rival gods may quarrel in the weather over the colony: rain and thunder on the storm's days, a hard clear sky on the other's, turn and turn about for a dozen days. An offering to one ends it sooner in that god's favour.
A god may ask the colony to speak against its rival to the rival's people, or to hide one the rival's people hunt for three days.
At supper one colonist may tell another a line of an old story of two gods the colony knows, and the story moves on as the history of their tie grows.

The Hunger answers anyone desperate enough: someone dying, someone at the edge of a breakdown, a colony out of food. It pays at once and plainly, and then it comes to take, more each time and sooner: a mark, years, a mind, a beast into the dark. The Choir of the Spire know its voice.

An archotech offers exact terms: so many goods past the gate within so many days, for exactly so much from orbit. The colony delivers when its stores hold them. It keeps its word, and does not forget a broken one.

The dead god's mark may be found cut into an old wall or wreck; the fading god asks to be remembered, gently or bitterly; the Sleeper asks for three things in dreams, and the third opens its door a crack; a newborn god of the colony's own gives its first small signs as it grows.
